title: AI voice clone scam call: what to do right now
h1: A loved one calls in a panic, asking for money. What to do right now.
desc: A crying voice that sounds like your child or parent, a crisis, a demand for money: it may be an AI voice clone. What to do in the next five minutes, how to check, how to report it, with real cases.
now: Hang up and call them back on a number you already have. Scammers can copy a voice from short audio clips, so the voice on the line proves nothing. Don't send money, gift cards or crypto while that call is still going. If your family has a safe word, ask for it.
steps: Hang up.
Don't argue and don't stay on the line. Keeping you talking is the scam: in one case reported this October, a California mother was kept on the phone for five hours while she wired $5,400.
Call them yourself, on a number you already have.
Not the number that called you. If they don't answer, call another relative or a friend who would know where they are.
Ask for your family's safe word.
A clone of their voice won't know it. If you don't have one yet, make one today.
Refuse payment by wire transfer, crypto or gift cards.
The FTC says requests to pay these ways are signs of a scam. Real emergencies don't need them.
If you already paid, act within the hour.
Call your bank or the transfer service and ask them to stop or reverse the payment. Then report it (below) and call your local police.
signs: An unknown or blocked number
Caller ID can also be faked, so a familiar name on screen isn't proof either.
Panic, crying, a crisis
An arrest, an accident, a kidnapping. Fear is designed to stop you thinking.
"Don't hang up" or "don't tell anyone"
Being cut off from everyone who could check the story is the point.
Wire, crypto or gift cards
Money that is fast to send and hard to get back.
The voice is right, but something is off
The FBI says to listen for tone and word choice that don't sound like your loved one.
prevent: Agree a family safe word.
A word or phrase only your family knows, kept off social media and texts. The FBI recommends it.
/shield/
Make one in two minutes
Limit public clips of your voice.
The FBI suggests keeping social media private and only accepting followers you know.
Tell the people most likely to be targeted.
Parents and grandparents especially. Send them this page.
stats: American adults scammed in 2025, losing about $68 billion, per a Gallup and Stop Scams Alliance survey; 12% of reported scams involved AI or deepfakes.
lost to impostor scams in 2025, from more than 1 million reports to the FTC. Total reported fraud losses hit a record $15.9 billion from 3 million reports.
of the scams in the Gallup survey were reported to the FTC or federal law enforcement. Most never are.
cases: A mother heard a cloned recording of her 37-year-old daughter crying for help, was told a cartel had kidnapped her, and wired $5,400 to Mexico over five hours. Her daughter was at work the whole time.
Police arrested two people over bank-helpdesk fraud that used AI-generated calls; about 170 victims and about €380,000 lost.
Police say a 23-year-old used AI voice cloning and deepfakes to pose as Elon Musk in a crypto 'trading' scam; nine arrested with UK, Canadian and German help.
Jennifer DeStefano got a call with what sounded like her teenage daughter sobbing, then a man demanding ransom. Her daughter was safe. She later testified about it to the US Senate.
report: The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center
the non-emergency number, or 911 if someone may really be in danger
faq: Can AI really copy someone's voice from a short clip?

Yes. The FBI warns that criminals use short audio clips to clone a relative's voice and ask for urgent money or ransom. A voice message, a video on social media or a few words on a call can be enough.
How can I tell if it's really them?
Don't try to judge the voice. Hang up and call them on a number you already have, ask for your family's safe word, or ask something only they would know that isn't online.
What is a family safe word?
A word or phrase agreed in person by your family and never posted or texted. In an emergency call you ask for it; a scammer with a cloned voice won't know it. The FBI recommends one.
I already sent money. What now?

Call your bank or the transfer service immediately and ask them to stop or reverse the payment. Then report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and the FBI at ic3.gov, and tell your local police. Recovery isn't guaranteed, and speed matters.
Where do I report an AI voice scam?
In the US: the FTC (ReportFraud.ftc.gov), the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (ic3.gov) and your local police. Reporting helps even if no money was lost.
Can caller ID be faked too?

Yes. It's called spoofing: a caller can make a different number, even a familiar one, show on your screen. So caller ID isn't proof. Call back on a number you already have. In the US you can report spoofed calls to the FCC at 1-888-225-5322.
sources: FTC: Scammers use AI to enhance their family emergency schemes (Mar 20, 2023)
FBI IC3: Criminals Use Generative Artificial Intelligence to Facilitate Financial Fraud (PSA I-120324, Dec 3, 2024)

aka: Also called the grandparent scam, the family emergency scam or virtual kidnapping.
script: If you ever get a call from me, or from anyone, saying I'm in trouble and need money, hang up and call me back on my usual number. If you can't reach me, call [another family member]. Ask for our safe word: ________. I will never ask you to pay with gift cards, wire transfers or crypto.

title: AI scam texts: how to spot them and what to do (2026)
h1: A text that seems off? How AI changed scam texts, and what to do
desc: Scam texts no longer have the typos that gave them away. The five most common text scams, the new AI-era warning signs, what to do if you clicked, and where to report it.
now: Don't tap the link and don't reply. If it claims to be your bank, a delivery or a toll, check by opening the company's own app or calling a number you already have. Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM), report it in your messaging app, and report fraud at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
intro: Bad spelling and clumsy grammar used to give scam texts away. The FBI warns that criminals now use AI to write persuasive messages faster, for more people, and to translate them without the errors that once exposed foreign scammers. The tell is no longer how a text is written. It's what the text wants you to do.
steps: Don't tap, don't reply.
Not even "STOP". The FTC's advice is never to click links in, or respond to, unexpected texts.
Check it another way.
Open the bank's, carrier's or delivery company's own app, or call a number you already have. Never use the link or number in the text.
Forward it to 7726.
That spells SPAM. It helps your mobile carrier block similar messages. Then use the report-junk option in iMessage or Google Messages.
Report it to the FTC.
At ReportFraud.ftc.gov. It takes a few minutes and feeds the data law enforcement uses.
If you clicked and typed anything in, act now.

Change that password, and anywhere you reuse it. Call your bank to block the card. If you shared ID details, go to IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan. If you sent money, call your bank and report it at ic3.gov.
types: Fake package delivery problems
A 'redelivery fee' link pretending to be the Postal Service or a courier. The most-reported text scam of 2024.
Fake jobs ('task scams')
Easy pay to rate apps or products, until you have to send money to 'finish your tasks' or unlock earnings.
Fake fraud alerts
Your 'bank' or Amazon about a suspicious charge, then pressure to move your money somewhere 'safe'. It goes to the scammer.
Bogus toll notices
An unpaid-toll balance with a link that collects card and Social Security numbers.
'Wrong number' texts
A friendly mistake that turns into a friendship, then an investment tip. Losses often run to tens of thousands of dollars.
signs: Urgency
Pay now, verify now, your account will close today.
A link or a number to call
Real companies rarely need you to act through a link in a text.
Moving your money 'to keep it safe'
No real bank asks you to move money to protect it.
'Let's move to WhatsApp, Signal or Telegram'
The FBI says impersonators use texts to move victims onto encrypted apps, sometimes using AI voice messages that sound like officials.
Perfect, friendly, patient writing
AI makes scam messages fluent and lets them keep chatting for weeks. Good writing isn't a sign of a real person.
stats: Texts were the most-reported way scammers first reached people in 2025, a year of record $15.9 billion in reported fraud losses.
lost to text scams in 2024, more than five times the 2020 figure. The FTC says most fraud is never reported.
cases: The FBI warned that impersonators sent texts and AI-cloned voice messages posing as senior US officials, moved targets onto encrypted apps, then texted their contacts too. It later said the campaign dated back to 2023.
A fan lost $10,000 to a fake 'Bon Jovi' who sent AI videos that said her name. The money requests began seven months after first contact.
Police say a 23-year-old used AI voice cloning and deepfakes to pose as Elon Musk in a crypto 'trading' scam.
report: The FBI, if you lost money
faq: Is it safe to reply STOP to a scam text?
No. The FTC's advice is not to respond to unexpected texts at all. Report the text and delete it. Replying STOP is for real companies you signed up with.
Can AI write scam texts?
Yes. The FBI warns that criminals use generative AI to write persuasive messages faster and for more people, and to translate them without the spelling and grammar mistakes that once gave them away.
What does forwarding to 7726 do?
7726 spells SPAM. Forwarding a scam text to it reports it to your mobile carrier, which uses the reports to block similar messages.
I clicked the link. What now?

If you didn't type anything, close it and don't go back. If you entered a password, change it everywhere you use it. If you entered card or bank details, call your bank. If you entered ID details such as a Social Security number, go to IdentityTheft.gov.
Are 'wrong number' texts scams?
Often. A friendly text to the wrong person is the classic opening of long scams that end in a fake investment. The FTC says these can cost tens of thousands of dollars.
Where do I report a scam text?
Forward it to 7726, use the report button in your messaging app, and report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If you lost money, also report it to the FBI at ic3.gov.
sources: FTC Data Spotlight: Top text scams of 2024 (Apr 2025)
FBI IC3: Criminals Use Generative Artificial Intelligence to Facilitate Financial Fraud (PSA I-120324, Dec 3, 2024)
CyberScoop: FBI says deepfake impersonation of US officials dates back to 2023 (Dec 2025)
FTC: What To Do if You Were Scammed
FTC testimony to the Joint Economic Committee on the scam economy (Mar 25, 2026)
aka: Also called smishing. The most common: fake delivery and redelivery-fee texts, fake toll bills, fake bank fraud alerts, job 'task' texts and 'wrong number' texts.

example.label: What one looks like (made-up example)
example.text: Your package could not be delivered due to an incomplete address. Update your details within 12 hours to avoid return: [link]
flags: No company you can check, and no tracking number you recognise
A deadline, so you act before you think
A link to 'update your details', which is where your card number goes

title: Fake AI nude of you or your child: what to do now
h1: Someone made a fake nude or sexual image of you, or your child, with AI. What to do now.
desc: An AI 'nudify' tool or chatbot turned an ordinary photo into a sexual image. It's not your fault, and there are free ways to get it taken down. What to do first, how to save evidence safely, where to report, and what the TAKE IT DOWN Act now requires of platforms.
aka: Also called deepfake nudes, 'nudify' or 'undress' images, nonconsensual intimate images (NCII) or image-based sexual abuse. When someone uses the image to demand money or more pictures, it's sextortion.
now: You did nothing wrong: the person who made or shared it did. If someone is demanding money or more pictures, don't pay and don't reply; block them, but keep the messages. Write down where the image is (links, usernames, dates) without forwarding it to anyone. Then get it taken down: NCMEC's Take It Down for anyone under 18, StopNCII for adults, and a removal request to each platform, which must now act within 48 hours.
intro: AI tools can turn an ordinary, fully clothed photo into a realistic sexual image in seconds. The FBI has warned since 2023 that criminals do this with pictures taken from social media, then post them or use them to harass and extort people, including children. A fake image can still do real harm, and it is treated seriously: the FBI says sexual images of children made with AI are illegal under federal law, and the TAKE IT DOWN Act covers AI deepfakes of adults too.
steps: Take a breath. This is not your fault.

The person who made or shared the image is responsible, not you and not your child. The FBI's message to victims: you are not alone, and this is not your fault. If it's your child, the first thing they need to hear from you is that they're not in trouble.
If someone is demanding money or more images: don't pay, don't reply.

The FBI and NCMEC both say paying or cooperating rarely stops the blackmail. Block the account and report it on the platform, but don't delete your profile or the messages: they help police find the person. Don't give anyone access to your accounts or devices, and be wary of companies that charge victims for 'removal' help; the FBI warns against them.
Save evidence, but don't spread the image.

Note or screenshot the web address, the usernames, the platform and the date and time of each post and message. The FBI asks victims to keep usernames, emails, platform names and messages. Don't forward or re-post the image, even to friends or to 'prove' it's fake. If the image appears to show someone under 18, don't copy, save or send the image itself: give the location to NCMEC and police and let them handle it.
Get it removed: under 18.

Use NCMEC's free Take It Down service. NCMEC says it can help whether an image is real or AI-made. It creates a digital fingerprint (a hash) on your device, so the picture is never uploaded, and participating platforms use it to find and remove copies. You can stay anonymous. It's for images of you when you were under 18, so adults can use it for those too. Also report the image on the CyberTipline with its exact web address.
Get it removed: 18 or over.

Use StopNCII.org, run by the UK's Revenge Porn Helpline. Its FAQ says deepfakes and manipulated images count, as long as you're the person shown and have a copy. Like Take It Down, it sends only a fingerprint to partner platforms, never the image. It works going forward; for images already online, report them to each site as well.
Report it to every platform it's on.

Use the report option next to the post, often under the three dots. Under the TAKE IT DOWN Act, social media, messaging and image or video sharing services must offer a way to request removal and take the image, and known identical copies, down within 48 hours of a valid request. If they don't, or you can't find a way to ask, report them to the FTC at TakeItDown.ftc.gov.
Report the person.

If the image shows a child: NCMEC's CyberTipline and the FBI (tips.fbi.gov or 1-800-CALL-FBI). For sextortion of anyone: the FBI, your local FBI field office or ic3.gov, and your local police. Many states also have their own laws against sexual deepfakes; police or a lawyer can tell you which apply where you live.
Get support, for you or your child.

Adults can call the Cyber Civil Rights Initiative's free 24/7 Image Abuse Helpline at 844-878-2274. Families of children can call NCMEC's 24-hour line, 1-800-843-5678, which can also help find someone to talk to. If anyone is having thoughts of self-harm, call or text 988 at any hour.
types: Under 18, or the image shows you when you were under 18
NCMEC's Take It Down (removal, anonymous) and CyberTipline (report). Call 1-800-843-5678 for help.
18 or over, and you have a copy of the image
StopNCII.org, which covers deepfakes of adults, plus a removal request to each platform.
Any age, the image is on a site or app
The platform's own report button. Under the TAKE IT DOWN Act it has 48 hours. If it ignores you: TakeItDown.ftc.gov.
Someone is threatening or blackmailing you
The FBI (tips.fbi.gov, 1-800-CALL-FBI or ic3.gov) and local police. Under 18: the CyberTipline too.
A platform won't act, or has no way to ask
The FTC at TakeItDown.ftc.gov. You can file for yourself, your child, or someone else with their permission.
prevent: Make social accounts private.

The FBI suggests private profiles and friends lists, and caution about posting photos of children publicly. It reduces the photos a stranger can grab, though it can't stop someone who already knows you.
https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2023/psa230605
FBI warning
Talk to your kids before it happens.

Tell them fake images exist, that it's never their fault, that paying a blackmailer doesn't work, and that they can come to you without being punished. NCMEC says teenage boys have been the most common targets of financial sextortion lately.
https://www.missingkids.org/theissues/sextortion
NCMEC on sextortion
Agree what your child should do if it ever happens.
Stop replying, don't pay, screenshot the account name, and tell you or another trusted adult. The FBI says sextortion can happen in as little as five minutes, so a plan made in advance matters.
Search for yourself now and then.
The FBI suggests using reverse image search to check whether your photos are circulating where they shouldn't be.
stats: reports to NCMEC's CyberTipline in 2025 involving generative AI, up from 67,000 in 2024 and 4,700 in 2023.
sexualized, photorealistic images estimated to have been posted by X's Grok in 11 days around New Year 2026, about 23,000 of them appearing to show children. An estimate from a 20,000-post sample.
is how long covered platforms have to remove a reported intimate image, and known identical copies, after a valid request. The rule took effect May 19, 2026.
cases: Police say a 41-year-old man photographed a teenage girl in a park and used Grok to turn the photo into abuse material; investigators report hundreds of AI-made images on his devices. He was arrested Oct 21 and has a hearing Oct 30. The charges are allegations.

A middle-school student allegedly made sexual deepfakes of several female classmates from ordinary photos and posted them online. Police opened an investigation after the images spread through the school.

Users prompted Grok to edit photos of real women and girls into sexualized images, often without consent. On Jan 9, after an outcry, xAI limited the image tools to paying users; several countries blocked Grok and regulators opened investigations.

A federal grand jury indicted a man accused of using Stable Diffusion to create thousands of sexual images of children. The Justice Department said AI-made abuse material will be prosecuted like any other.
Explicit AI fakes of Taylor Swift spread widely before removal; one post was seen tens of millions of times. It showed how fast a fake can travel, even for someone with a large team behind her.
report: NCMEC's CyberTipline, if the image shows a child
NCMEC's Take It Down, to remove images of under-18s
StopNCII, to stop images of adults spreading
The FBI, for sextortion or images of children
The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center
The FTC, if a platform won't take it down within 48 hours
the non-emergency number, or 911 if someone is in danger
faq: Is it illegal to make a fake nude of someone with AI?

For images of children, yes: the FBI says sexual images of minors made with generative AI are illegal under federal law, including realistic computer-generated ones. For adults, the federal TAKE IT DOWN Act makes publishing nonconsensual intimate images a crime and covers AI deepfakes, and many states have their own laws. Which charges apply depends on what was made, shared and where.
What is the TAKE IT DOWN Act?

A federal law signed on May 19, 2025. Since May 19, 2026, social media, messaging and image or video sharing platforms must give people a way to ask for nonconsensual intimate images to be removed, and must take them down, with known identical copies, within 48 hours of a valid request. It covers real images, edited ones and AI deepfakes. The FTC enforces it.
The platform hasn't removed it after 48 hours. What now?

Report the platform to the FTC at TakeItDown.ftc.gov. You can also report it if you can't find a removal process or it doesn't work. You can file if you or your child are in the image, or for someone else with their permission.
Do I have to send the image to get it removed?

No. Take It Down and StopNCII both create a digital fingerprint on your own device and share only that, never the image. Take It Down lets you stay anonymous. For an image of a child, don't send or save copies yourself: give the web address to the CyberTipline or police.
Someone says they'll post a fake of me unless I pay. Should I pay?

No. The FBI says cooperating rarely stops the blackmail, but law enforcement can. Stop replying, block them, keep the messages and usernames, report the account to the platform and contact the FBI or local police. If you're under 18, tell a trusted adult and report to NCMEC too.
My teenager made one of a classmate. What should I do?

Take it seriously and act fast. Make sure they delete it from every device and account and don't share it further, and talk to the school. A sexual image of a minor is illegal even if it's AI-made, so get legal advice. The classmate's family can use Take It Down and the CyberTipline to get it removed.
Will it ever be fully gone?

Often most copies can be taken down, but there's no guarantee. Take It Down and StopNCII only work on participating, public or unencrypted platforms, and edited or cropped versions may need to be submitted separately. NCMEC also explains how to ask Google and Bing to drop cached copies from search results.
Where can I talk to someone?

Adults: the Cyber Civil Rights Initiative's free 24/7 Image Abuse Helpline, 844-878-2274. Children and families: NCMEC, 1-800-843-5678. If you or your child are thinking about self-harm, call or text 988, any time.
script: If anyone ever sends you a picture that looks like you, or says they'll share one unless you pay or send more: stop replying, don't pay, screenshot their username, and come to me. You won't be in trouble. It wouldn't be your fault, and we'll fix it together.

title: Is this video real? How to check before you share
h1: Is this video real? How to check a clip before you share it
desc: A shocking video of a candidate, a celebrity or someone you know may be an AI deepfake. Eight checks that take a few minutes, what not to rely on, and where to report it.
aka: Also called deepfakes, AI-generated video, synthetic media or 'cheapfakes' when real footage is edited.
now: Don't share it yet. Find where it first appeared, search whether major news outlets or fact-checkers have confirmed it, and check who posted it. If it's about voting, get the facts only from your state or local election office or vote.gov.
intro: You can't reliably spot a good deepfake by looking at it. The checks that work are about where a clip came from and who has confirmed it, not about pixels. They take a few minutes, and they work for election clips, celebrity 'endorsements' and videos of people you know.
steps: Pause before you share.
If a clip makes you angry or shocked, slow down. That is exactly when fakes spread fastest.
Find where it first came from.
Ask who posted it first and where. A brand-new or anonymous account is a warning sign; the account behind the Talarico deepfake was created only a month earlier.
Reverse-search a screenshot.
Take a screenshot of a key frame and upload it to Google Images or TinEye to find the original and see whether it was edited.
See what trusted outlets say.
Leave the post and search for the claim. If something this big were real, several news outlets or fact-checkers would be reporting it, or the campaign would have confirmed it.
Look and listen for glitches.
Check whether lips match the words, and watch for odd blinking, warped edges or backgrounds, and a flat or slurred voice. Newer fakes may show none of these signs, so this is only one clue.
Check for Content Credentials.
Upload an image or paste its link into contentcredentials.org/verify to see any record of the tool used, including AI. A missing credential does not prove a file is fake.
Read the fine print on ads.
Check who paid for an ad (usually stated at the end) and look for an AI disclaimer. Many states require one, but most AI ads this year carried none.
Get voting details only from officials.
Don't click links in unexpected texts or emails about your registration. Check with your state or county election office instead.
types: Your eyes alone
Lip-sync errors, odd blinking and warped backgrounds are worth noticing, but the best fakes don't have them, and real videos can look glitchy.
AI 'deepfake detector' apps
Results vary widely and can be wrong in both directions. Treat them as one clue, never as proof.
The number of views or shares
Bots can inflate both; Bloomberg reports bot-boosted views on the Matryoshka operation's fake celebrity videos.
A verified badge or familiar name
Accounts can be bought, hacked or impersonated. Check the account's history and when it was created.
signs: It makes you furious or thrilled
Fakes are built to trigger a fast share. Strong emotion is the cue to slow down.
A brand-new or anonymous account posted it first
The account behind a deepfake of Texas Senate candidate James Talarico had been created about a month earlier.
No major outlet is reporting it
If a candidate really said something explosive, newsrooms would be covering it within hours.
It tells you to vote differently
A clip or message changing your polling place, date or method is a red flag. Check with your election office.
It's an ad with no 'paid for by' line, or no AI disclosure
Many states require AI disclosures in political ads, but most AI ads this cycle didn't carry one.
stats: The Wesleyan Media Project counted at least 220 political ads made or enhanced with AI by Oct 11, costing just under $137 million, against less than $50,000 of AI ad spending in the 2024 presidential election.
Of those 220 ads, only 27% told viewers AI was used. 81% were paid for by Republican candidates or groups and 12% by pro-Democratic sponsors.
More than 4 in 10 voters say an AI ad fooled them

In a Scripps News/Talker Research poll of 1,000 registered voters (Sept 30–Oct 1), more than four in ten said they had seen something in a political ad they thought was real and later learned was AI. Another 30% weren't sure. The headline says 43%.
cases: Videos posted on X showed a man falsely accusing Senate candidate James Talarico; researchers judged them 'very likely' deepfakes, linked to the Russia-aligned Storm-1516 operation. PolitiFact rated the claim Pants on Fire and X suspended the account.
A county judge's campaign shared, then pulled, an AI-generated video of Black residents endorsing him.
An AI clone of President Biden's voice in robocalls told voters to stay home from the primary.
report: The platform where you saw it
use its report button for manipulated or misleading media
Your state or local election office
if it gives false voting information (find yours at vote.gov)
if it's being used in a scam, such as fake donation appeals
faq: How can you tell if a video is a deepfake?

Don't rely on spotting glitches; good fakes don't have obvious ones. Check where the clip first appeared, whether major outlets or fact-checkers have confirmed it, and who posted it. A brand-new or anonymous account posting something explosive is a warning sign.
Can I check a video with a deepfake detector?
You can try, but detectors are unreliable and can be wrong in both directions. Use them as one clue at most. Where a clip came from, and who has confirmed it, matters more.
What are Content Credentials?

A labelling standard (C2PA) that some cameras, apps and AI tools use to record how an image or video was made. You can upload a file at contentcredentials.org/verify. If there's no record, that doesn't prove it's fake or real.
Are AI political ads legal?

In most states, yes, with conditions. NCSL counted 31 states regulating election deepfakes as of June 2026, most by requiring a disclosure. There's no federal law on AI in campaign ads; AI-voiced robocalls fall under federal robocall rules.
What should I do if I've already shared a fake?
Delete it, and post a short correction where you shared it. That stops it spreading further and helps the people who saw it from you.
Where do I report an election deepfake?
Report it on the platform. If it gives false voting information, tell your state or local election office.
sources: Find where it first came from (source)
Read the fine print on ads (source)
